content: Misoprostol, when administered via the buccal or sublingual routes, has distinct pharmacokinetic advantages. The oral and sublingual routes allow for a rapid onset of action, while the sublingual and vaginal routes provide prolonged activity and higher bioavailability. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of buccal or sublingual misoprostol for cervical ripening and induction of labor during the third trimester. The search for relevant studies included databases such as the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, with updates performed in 2009. Randomized controlled trials comparing buccal or sublingual misoprostol to placebo, no treatment, or other labor induction methods were included. Data from these trials were extracted, verified for accuracy, and analyzed using standardized methodologies and RevMan software. Three studies involving a total of 502 participants were included in the analysis. These studies compared buccal or sublingual misoprostol with vaginal and oral regimens. When comparing the buccal route to the vaginal route (200 µg versus 50 µg), there was a trend toward fewer cesarean sections in the buccal group (18 out of 73 versus 28 out of 79 participants; relative risk [RR] 0.70; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.42 to 1.15). However, no significant differences were observed in other outcomes. When the same dosage of misoprostol was administered sublingually versus orally, the sublingual route showed a trend toward fewer failures to achieve vaginal delivery within 24 hours (12 out of 50 versus 19 out of 50 participants; RR 0.63; 95% CI 0.34 to 1.16), reduced need for oxytocin augmentation (17 out of 50 versus 23 out of 50 participants; RR 0.74; 95% CI 0.45 to 1.21), and fewer cesarean sections (8 out of 50 versus 15 out of 50 participants; RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.25 to 1.14). However, these differences were not statistically significant. When a smaller dose was used sublingually compared to orally, no differences in outcomes were observed. The authors concluded that, based on the limited data from three small trials, sublingual misoprostol appears to be at least as effective as oral administration when the same dose is used. However, there is insufficient evidence to assess the relative risks of complications and side effects. Larger trials are necessary to establish the safety and optimal dosage of sublingual or buccal misoprostol before it can be recommended for clinical use. Additionally, the 17 citations awaiting classification in this review may influence the conclusions once they are assessed.
